note_tweet.text:
Meta is quietly changing the way we think about AI assistants. And I find this direction much more interesting than another chatbot update.

Meet Spaces, a new feature for Meta's Muse agents.
@Muse

The idea is surprisingly simple. Instead of having one endless conversation with AI, you describe what you want to achieve, and Muse builds a dedicated space around that goal.

Planning a vacation? Create a travel planner.
Organizing a family event? Build a recipe and shopping tracker.
Managing projects? Let Muse create a dashboard and keep everything organized.

But here's where things get really interesting.

Spaces can connect to third-party apps and update information in the background. Concert dates change, prices move, savings grow, and Muse can keep your workspace updated without you having to ask every time.

Mark Zuckerberg says he's already experimented with a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard.

And this is only the beginning.

I think we're moving toward a future where software will be built less around menus, buttons and complicated interfaces, and more around what people actually want to accomplish.

You won't necessarily need to learn how to use five different apps. You'll simply describe the result you want, and your AI agent will build the environment to help you get there.

That's a pretty big shift.

But there's another side to this future that deserves attention.

The more useful these agents become, the more access they'll need to our calendars, emails, finances, purchases and personal information. Convenience is attractive, but trust, privacy and control will become just as important as intelligence.

Maybe the next big technology competition won't be about who has the smartest chatbot.

It will be about who can build the most useful personal agent, one that understands your goals, remembers what matters and actually gets things done without taking control away from you.

And perhaps one day, we'll stop thinking of AI as something we open when we need an answer.

It will simply be there, quietly working alongside us.

The question is no longer just what AI can tell us. It's what we are ready to let it do.

#AI #Meta #Muse #Agents #FutureOfWork

🔥☕ The This Is Fine Trade
@chamath @DavidSacks @dhh @DowdEdward 

The room is on fire. Export controls. Federal AI bans. A US–China race over chips, models and who gets to build on what. And the market is sitting at the table, sipping coffee, saying “this is fine.”

Here’s my thesis: geopolitics is quietly repricing which AI models enterprises can actually use, and the market hasn’t caught up.

The trade

LONG Western open weights
$NVDA (Nemotron)
$META (Muse Spark Open)
$ASML (Mistral’s largest shareholder)

SHORT Chinese open weights
https://t.co/p6R9UOz9OK (Zhipu, maker of GLM)
https://t.co/SVlLSwgWJp (MiniMax)

Why
Chinese open models are genuinely good and very cheap. On raw token cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is the cheapest model I priced: about $13k a year for a team-scale coding-agent workload of 2B input and 400M output tokens a month.

But cheap tokens aren’t the whole bill. 

DeepSeek is already barred from federal civilian IT and from DoD contract work. A Senate defense bill would extend that to ten more Chinese AI companies and any models built on theirs. 

If your compliance team forces a model swap mid-project, re-engineering and re-testing costs real money. I used $250k.

Price that risk in, measure quality by coding score, and the ranking flips:

Risk-adjusted $ per coding point
Mistral Large 4: $727
Nemotron 3 Ultra: $953
Muse Spark Open: $1,291
GLM-5.3: $1,987
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: $2,021
Kimi K3.1 Pro: $2,607
Claude Opus 5.5: $3,244
Gemini 4 Argon: $3,511
GPT-6 Astra: $9,116

Western open weights are close to the Chinese models on coding, a fraction of the price of the closed frontier labs, and legally safe to build on. 

For regulated and government-adjacent enterprises, that’s the winning combination.

The “this is fine” part

The market prices Chinese AI labs on benchmarks and token prices. It doesn’t price the moment a US enterprise’s compliance team says no. That gap is the trade.

What kills it

I’d rather say this up front than have it pointed out in the replies:

Zhipu and MiniMax earn most of their revenue in China, where US procurement bans don’t apply.

NVDA, META and ASML move on chips, ads and lithography, not on open-model adoption. This is a thematic expression, not a pure play.

A US–China deal could reverse policy overnight.
Shorting Hong Kong stocks is restricted to designated securities, and borrowing may be costly or unavailable.
The risk probabilities in my model are judgment, not data.

Run your own numbers

The fundamental Risk Adjusted Enterprise ROI full model is a spreadsheet: change the workload, the risk percentages and the migration cost, and every number updates.

e. Call & Letter

Dictating Deal Terms – Pricing, Duration & Structure:

To give an idea of how favorable the multi-year demand backdrop currently is, deal size and duration both continued to rise despite NBIS introducing new ways to add short-term capacity. They’re dictating terms and notching ongoing megawatt pricing power. For context, last quarter, NBIS disclosed pricing per megawatt jumped from a little over $10M at the time of the spin-off to $22.5M on new deals. This quarter, that again ticked higher to $25M+.

On one end, as briefly mentioned, NBIS is introducing various market models to offer short-term compute. This helps them take full advantage of the vast supply/demand mismatch, often fetching over $40M per megawatt for these more temporary deals. They’re now letting customers bid for blocks of guaranteed capacity and renting out idle chips at spot rates without large commitments or long-term lock-ins. NBIS has enticing flexibility to make this capacity available when it’s able to, and quickly pull it when reserved demand requires them to do so.

• These two methods complement 3-6 month cluster commitment offerings.

Along with on-demand and short-term clusters, these give customers more ways in the door and give Nebius a live read on demand. Early results are encouraging. Reserve auctions closed 15%+ above the minimum price. Both winners were brand-new customers, and the first has already grown its contract value 10x.

• They see many short-term and spot-capacity users graduate into 1-3 year contracts, which is their bread and butter.
• They’re also seeing plenty of pay-per-token customers on shared servers moving up to reserve larger dedicated compute clusters.
• Remember when leadership told us last quarter that it was holding back capacity to fetch better terms? It worked. In early September, it released a new batch of capacity with higher prices, longer commitments and more cash required upfront.
• Longer term, the plan is to run all of this through a single trading platform that automatically toggles pricing and terms for all customers.

Nebius is also enjoying stronger 5-year contract demand for Nebius AI Cloud (not just dedicated deals with mega-caps). These deals are long, large and typically prepaid all at once. Customers lock in today’s rates during a time when GPU prices continue to soar. Nebius gets better visibility and a sub-2-year payback period.

Capacity – Footprint Updates:

Q3 was Nebius’s biggest quarter ever for adding active capacity. Four new sites across the U.S. and Europe started producing revenue, and New Jersey got more tranches in Q3 and into November. More is coming in Q4, including new colocation phases in the U.S., Europe and Israel. It’s at 4+ GW of contracted power today and still expects 5 GW by year-end. As a reminder, contracted power is not operating capacity. It’s secured access to electricity. The buildings, cooling, networking and chips still have to show up before a customer can use any of it.

• Missouri, 2 Finland sites and Alabama are expected to add operational capacity in 2027. These will ramp to 3+ GW by sometime in 2030. Pennsylvania is also under construction and should begin contributing after that.

Capacity – Geographic Expansion:

In terms of geographic footprint expansion, Asia-Pacific is going well about 6 months after launching. Customer contracts have been signed across Korea, Japan, India, Australia and Singapore and they’ve hired managers in Korea and Japan to spur more growth. Its first two facilities in the region will be colocation projects in India. Both are expected to start operating in 2027, which is when regional revenue should start to scale.

Moving into more parts of the globe is vital for NBIS’s value proposition. On one hand, governments want to run their AI infrastructure locally to help with tight data controls and easier security. NBIS can provide that, with localized go-to-market across Europe (and now APAC) that lawmakers and core suppliers like Nvidia find valuable. Speaking of Nvidia, they also get to use NBIS to cut through project red tape and expedite regulatory procedures with their more local knowledge. Every country handles data residency, chip export rules and permitting differently. It’s annoying, hectic and inconsistent. Nvidia obviously wants its chips everywhere, and it’s much easier to get there through local, independent cloud partners that already have the sites, power and approvals than to do it alone. That’s part of why Nvidia invests in companies like Nebius and hands them new hardware early. NBIS is happy to be the soldier, considering how much money they expect to make from these AI factories.

• Palantir naming it a preferred cloud partner for its sovereign AI customers is more good evidence. Palantir will pair its Foundry platform with Token Factory and open models to serve those customers.

Capacity – Mix Shift to Owned:

So demand is insatiable, pricing is rising… and Nebius still cut its revenue guide. Why? The capacity didn’t arrive on time. A number of colocation sites are now slated for delivery in the first half of 2027. According to leadership, this is purely timing-related. Nothing was canceled. They proactively communicated this with customers and expect the delays to be short-lived. In August, DataOne, a key New Jersey facility partner, told NBIS the original generator plan wouldn’t work, forcing a switch to cleaner, behind-the-meter Bloom Energy fuel cells. DataOne’s temporary generators were supposed to bridge the gap while Bloom ramped, but it wound them down faster than expected. That gap caused the delay. Again… high degree of execution risk here.

• NBIS plans to use Bloom at its other sites too.

All of this is even more strongly motivating NBIS to prioritize owned facilities over colocations. This is how they pocket a larger piece of the profit pie. This is how they control delivery schedules, with all owned NBIS facilities currently on time. This format also grants more flexibility to scale up capacity or slow down expansion if the backdrop softens for whatever reason. It does mean a lot more CapEx to get projects online, but once that’s incurred, they get all of these benefits in addition to higher-margin business. Nebius also designs its own racks and storage, and leadership expects those costs to keep falling as more capacity comes from owned sites. As seen below, NBIS plans to rapidly shift to this format going forward, and it already has “all power and components secured” for its 2027 demand plan. And yes… that includes Nvidia’s next-gen hardware. Supply of Vera CPUs, Vera Rubin GPUs and Groq chips is confirmed for 2027, with testing and benchmarking now done.

More on Strong Customers:

Nebius has $40B+ in committed revenue from investment-grade customers, led by Microsoft and Meta. Microsoft signed a contract worth $17.4B to $19.4B in September 2025. Meta signed for $3B that November and added up to $27B more this March ($12B committed, plus up to $15B for capacity Nebius doesn’t sell to others first).

Why are these backstops so much more comforting than one from OpenAI or Anthropic? Because of who’s writing the check. Microsoft and Meta are two of the most profitable companies on the planet, with pristine credit ratings. The AI labs are growing at an incredible pace, but they’re still far more dependent on external capital to honor multi-year compute contracts. If funding markets tighten, that’s a problem for whoever built capacity for them. Lenders see the difference too. It’s why Nebius can borrow against these contracts at SOFR + 2.50%. That’s exactly what it did in July with a $775M facility, which is the first under what leadership calls a “repeatable framework.” Other hyperscaler-backed GPU loans price similarly (SOFR + 2.25% for both CoreWeave’s Meta-backed facility and IREN’s Microsoft-backed one), while CoreWeave’s 2026 loans backed by AI labs and smaller customers priced at SOFR + 4.50% to 5.50%. At the same time, this also invites concentration risk. Two customers make up most of the backlog. And as our Amazon review covered, hyperscalers earn much lower margins renting from neoclouds than using their own sites. They’re here because they’re short on capacity. When that shortage ends, renewals are no guarantee. The good news? These are 5-year contracts and new TCV is increasingly coming from AI natives and enterprise platforms like Databricks. The base is diversifying.

More on Depreciation & Payback Period:

Ignoring prepayments and considering all costs, expected payback on comparable 1-3 year deals shortened from 22 months to 19 months Q/Q. That’s so important. GPUs cost a fortune and depreciate far more quickly than other assets like the data center buildings. These being useful for 60 months means NBIS has 41 months of profits to collect. That 41 months is worth north of $85M of revenue per megawatt at current contract pricing… with most of that revenue flowing down to net income. Anything this company can do to shrink payback periods by even a single month is worth roughly $2M in added profit per megawatt, and stretching useful lives has the same impact.

In fairness, there’s a counterargument. Old chips are holding value because compute is scarce. If supply catches up with demand, the oldest and least power-efficient chips lose pricing power first. And if power becomes the bottleneck, newer chips that produce more tokens per watt can justify swapping old ones out early. I wouldn’t pencil in 7 or 8 years. But 5 looks safe.

Platform Innovation – Inference (Token Factory), Post-Training & Agent Execution:

As mentioned, run rate here is approaching multi-hundred-million-dollar levels while contract value rose 17x Q/Q with compelling profitability. Margins are notably favorable compared to other inference providers due to NBIS's direct chip ownership. To keep nurturing the momentum, it purchased EigenAI to increase tokens-per-chip throughput while also buying Inferize last month to fix the “cold start” problem (slow model loading when demand spikes). That will allow chip utilization rates to rise further and NBIS performance dynamics to improve too.

• Kimi K3, Meta Muse Spark Open and others were available the day they came out.
• Artificial Analysis benchmarks put Token Factory in the top tier for performance, latency and quality on the latest DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM models.
• Per leadership, open-source model adoption has accelerated in recent months. As an agnostic place to run any model, they prefer fragmentation and the complexity that coincides with it. They can provide more value in this environment.
• For context, OpenRouter said open-weight models made up 72% of its weekly token volume in September. It first crossed 50% in February.

Next is post-training. Some quick reminders. Training is building a model from scratch. Inference is using that model to conduct work. Post-training is ongoing upgrades to existing models to make them better. Examples include fine-tuning it on a company’s own data, and teaching it through trial and error. To avoid model lock-in, customers can easily transfer that progress to a different model if they find a cheaper option. And importantly, on NBIS, customers can do all of this while running their inference engines and accessing a full suite of software in one single place. It’s a routine sale too, as the infrastructure (training clusters and Token Factory) is already there. Applied Compute and Cursive both post-trained custom models on Nebius AI Cloud, then picked Token Factory for inference.

Finally, like we’ve talked about in other AI infrastructure reviews, agent execution requires a lot of CPU-based compute too. GPUs are incredibly powerful, but they need clear instruction and orchestration, and that’s where CPUs come into play. So Nebius is adding CPU capacity next to its GPUs, including those early Vera CPU deployments. CPU-rich work generally means higher margins too, and it opens up a wide array of potential enterprise agent services to enrich margins and returns. This is why Tavily is so important. Giving agents the search tools needed to fetch timely information and insight is a big part of ensuring outputs are high-quality just like CPU-based presence is.

More Notes:

• Regulation: Nebius doesn’t expect midterms to affect its greenfield or colocation sites, Pennsylvania included. It has sites live or under construction in roughly half a dozen states (Texas isn’t one). And per leadership, data center pushback is coming from both sides of the aisle… not just one party.
• Avride (autonomous vehicles): Avride now has 250 vehicles on the road and wants 350 by the end of the year. It has logged more than 2M autonomous miles and over 100K robotaxi trips. Its Dallas coverage area is 3x larger, and fully driverless service should start by June 2027. On the delivery side, its robots now make more than 6,500 deliveries per day, over 3x more than a year ago.
• Toloka (AI data; equity stake): Revenue doubled Q/Q and it launched a post-training offering.
• ClickHouse (database; equity stake): No update beyond its January raise at a roughly $15B valuation.

note_tweet.text:
If every agent you run lives on one platform, you have a single point of failure without any control. 

When usage gets throttled or capabilities change you are stuck or left scrambling.

Not to mention different agents have different specialty use cases, which make them better than others in their niche. (Grok Bot for X, Muse for Meta, Duet for Claude, etc...)

You need to be diversifying the platforms you build workflows on, and now its incredibly easy to do.

(HOW TO DIVERSIFY) 3 tips + 1 bonus tip

1. Map where your work runs

List every job your agents do in a week. Next to each one, write the platform it runs on. If one name fills most of the column, that's your exposure.

2. Sort the list into locked v.s off-board

Locked jobs need something only Grok has. Think about what each agents specialty use case is. GrokBot is amazing for X research, multi-agent coordination, browser use etc...

Off-board workflows that you feel comfortable moving away from GrokBot and on to other agents (Muse, Hermes, etc...)

3. Move the jobs asap

Do it while nothing is broken.

Using https://t.co/xwQeBgCauG create a group chat with your GrokBot agent and your other agents (Muse, Dots, Hermes etc..) and have GrokBot train it on its task.

We had GrokBot teach a free Meta Muse agent (or two🤫) and we also onboarded @OpenBot_  into our ecosystem. (We love it. @norbertbodziony)

BONUS TIP Give the group your projects context through a shared vault

Now that you have your agents diversified and communicating in one group chat, give them a shared vault that holds the context of your project so they can easily work together to accomplish tasks for you.

Final word: We run agents across nearly all major platforms everyday. We share what that teaches us while we learn. Follow along.

I let an AI agent run most of my life for 60 days.

His name is Carl. He's my Meta @Muse agent, and he handles 40+ jobs for me now: groceries and meal prep, two email inboxes, shopping, playlists, fitness, finances, etc.

He's really good. He also tried to pay a $70 hazmat fee on a $15 order and thought that was fine. So he's not perfect.

In this video, I gave him an honest report card and also shared which other agents perform better in each scenario:

01:36 Voice mode. Can you actually talk to your agent while doing dishes or driving? Is it fast enough to feel like a real conversation? Can it handle a few tasks at once, or does it go quiet?

04:56 Shopping. Can it find the exact part you need, or does it guess? Can it pay for you safely without getting played at checkout? And can it buy something on Amazon?

09:56 Email. Can you connect more than one inbox? Can you control which permissions it has and what it can or cannot do? Does it just triage, or does it actually suggest what to do next?

12:35 Groceries. Can it plan a family's whole week from a few fridge photos? Does it work around everyone's schedule and my daughter's school lunch? Can my wife use it with me?

16:09 Portability. Can your agent follow you to any device, with all its memory? What about glasses and new hardware?

17:23 Images and video. Can it make a 60-second trailer that actually makes sense? Do the clips match each other and the script?

Most rounds went better than I expected. One got a 4 out of 10.

21:21 The verdict, the one thing I still won't trust it with, and which agent I'd pick instead for each job.

It's one of the better agent roundups you'll find. Even if you're not using @Muse yet, it's worth seeing how good of a job these agents actually do in real-life scenarios.

Full report card in the video below 👇

Across the entire AI travel industry, consumers happily use chatbots to brainstorm vacations but still refuse to trust an algorithm with their credit card.

Odessia proved this gap when tens of thousands of early users planned over 60 million dollars in annualized trips on the platform, yet that headline figure measured unpaid wishlists rather than actual booked revenue. 

When OpenAI bought the 9 person startup on November 10 and shut it down just 27 days after its public launch, the deal exposed how every AI travel player hits the exact same wall between casual daydreaming and real checkout.

Even Odessia stopped short of full automation during its brief life because complex date changes still confused the system. After the AI filtered hundreds of flights and hotels in a minute, it still forced the human user to manually type in a verification code and click the final purchase button.

Late 2026 operating numbers across the wider travel industry show that this trust gap between high intent research and completed checkout is universal:

> Uber: AI agents booked a grand total of 4 rides across the entire platform during its busiest week in October 2026.

> Booking Holdings: AI assistant users on Priceline and Agoda convert at 2 times the normal rate, yet external AI channels drive well under 1% of total room nights.

> Tripadvisor and Viator: AI referrals convert at nearly 5 times the site average on Viator, even as total AI booking volume remains small.

> OpenTable and OpenAI: ChatGPT seated 190,000 diners in September 2026, representing just 0.12% of OpenTable's 158.3 million monthly diners, months after OpenAI pulled back on its own native checkout.

While most AI travel startups like Expedia acquisition Layla simply generate text itineraries and link out to traditional booking sites, Odessia separated itself from early clones by building three local defenses.

An 8 to 9 person team shipped a low latency platform in 5 months, applied for an IATA travel agency license in week one to unlock perks at 2,000 luxury hotels, and scanned years of users' Gmail inboxes and Google calendars to build a sticky personal memory.

Yet those clever startup defenses offered only a brief window of survival rather than a permanent moat against internet and travel giants:

> Booking and Expedia: Booking holds 4.4 million properties with mid 60% direct traffic and high 50% loyalty room nights, while both giants spend between 7.35 billion and 8.19 billion dollars a year on marketing.

> Google AI Mode: Launched in August 2026, it connects directly to Hilton, Marriott, IHG, and major booking sites with built in Google Pay checkout.

> Meta Muse: Released in September 2026, the assistant hit 730,000 downloads in 5 days and pulls live inventory straight from Expedia and https://t.co/Dd6iN35qpS.

> ChatGPT: Over 1.2 billion weekly active users already treat the chatbot as a default daily tool for trip planning.

With no exclusive hotel rooms and no cheap traffic pool, pushing Odessia beyond tens of thousands of early geeks meant crashing straight into an 8 billion dollar ad wall and native big tech features.

Odessia avoided getting crushed not because its moat was unbeatable, but because it packaged its supply chain credentials and team into OpenAI right before its short window closed.

Looking at your own segment, can an AI application startup actually survive a head on war against incumbent giants, or is packaging yourself into a big tech ecosystem during a brief showcase window the only smart exit left?

If you have seen a young contender build a moat strong enough to fight the giants alone, which one is proving this wrong? https://t.co/fYBg6aZHti
